metadata.title: Got math attitude? (In)direct effects of student mathematics attitudes on intentions, behavioral engagement, and mathematics performance in the U.S. PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the U.S. PISA 2012 public-use dataset, where the complex survey design is intended to support population generalization. For descriptive statistics and composite/indicator summaries, the authors report using the final student weight (WFSTUWT) in SPSS. For the SEM analyses predicting intentions, behavioral engagement, and mathematics performance, they use replicate weights via Mplus REPWEIGHT with 80 replicate weight variables (WFSTR1–WFSTR80) to adjust standard errors for sampling variance. The SEM also incorporates the five mathematics plausible values simultaneously (TYPE = Imputation), and the authors use WLSMV for categorical indicators; no alternative unweighted ML pipeline is described.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is the U.S. PISA 2012 public-use dataset downloaded from NCES. The study uses the mathematics domain as the focus because mathematics performance is the competency domain in 2012. The authors report that the rotated questionnaire design yields a large proportion of missing background questionnaire data (>2/3), which they treat as missing completely at random (MCAR) and therefore do not apply multiple imputation to background variables; instead, they estimate SEM parameters using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus with all available data. For mathematics performance, they use the five plausible values provided in the national database and estimate the SEM with TYPE = Imputation, accounting for plausible-value uncertainty. No additional country filtering is described beyond restricting to the U.S. sample.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (WLSMV) with five plausible values; explained variance R² = 0.307 (SE = 0.013), p < 0.001. Direct effect: Behavioral engagement → Math performance β = 0.255 (SE = 0.016), p < 0.001. Indirect effect: Perceived behavioral control → Math performance through behavior β = 0.184 (SE = 0.014), p < 0.001. Indirect effects via intentions: Intention → Math performance (through behavior) β = 0.015 (SE = 0.005), p = 0.003; Attitude → Math performance via intention,behavior β = 0.006 (SE = 0.018), p = 0.009; Subjective norms → Math performance via intention,behavior β = -0.001 (SE = 0.000), p = 0.010.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics (U.S. 15-year-olds) the study leveraged attitude, perceived behavioral control, intentions, and behavioral engagement (controlling for gender, race/ethnicity, and ESCS) to predict mathematics performance (plausible values), finding that behavioral engagement had a positive direct effect (β = 0.255) and perceived behavioral control improved performance indirectly through behavioral engagement (β = 0.184), while intentions had only a weak indirect contribution. This indicates that interventions should prioritize strengthening students’ day-to-day mathematics work ethic and self-efficacy/control beliefs rather than relying primarily on long-term intentions to pursue mathematics.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Explained variance R² = 0.211 (SE = 0.013), p < 0.001. Direct effects: Attitude → Intentions β = 0.420 (SE = 0.026), p < 0.001; Subjective norms → Intentions β = -0.083 (SE = 0.030), p < 0.05; Perceived behavioral control → Intentions β = 0.058 (SE = 0.039), p = 0.132. Demographic effects: Gender (female vs male) β = -0.324 (SE = 0.028), p < 0.001; ESCS effect on intentions β = -0.035 (SE = 0.020), p = 0.086 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics (U.S. 15-year-olds) the study leveraged attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control (controlling for gender, race/ethnicity, and ESCS) to predict intentions to pursue mathematics, finding that attitude had a strong positive direct effect (β = 0.420) while subjective norms had a small negative effect (β = -0.083) and perceived behavioral control was not significant (β = 0.058). This indicates that improving students’ perceived value and usefulness of mathematics is likely to be more effective for shaping intentions than increasing social-pressure messages or relying on control beliefs alone.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Explained variance R² = 0.594 (SE = 0.022), p < 0.001. Direct effects: Perceived behavioral control → Behavior β = 0.719 (SE = 0.018), p < 0.001; Intentions → Behavior β = 0.064 (SE = 0.019), p < 0.05. Attitude → Behavior indirect effect via intentions reported as β = 0.027 (SE = 0.009), p = 0.009 (total indirect). Demographic effects: ESCS → Behavior β = 0.178 (SE = 0.021), p < 0.001; Gender (female vs male) β = 0.223 (SE = 0.029), p < 0.001.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics (U.S. 15-year-olds) the study leveraged perceived behavioral control and intentions (with attitude and demographic controls) to predict behavioral engagement (mathematics work ethic), finding that perceived behavioral control had the strongest positive direct effect (β = 0.719) and intentions had a small positive effect (β = 0.064). This indicates that classroom practices that build self-efficacy and controllability for mathematics tasks are likely to yield the largest improvements in students’ mathematics work ethic, with intentions playing a secondary role.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes the U.S. sample of PISA 2012, focusing on mathematics performance (five plausible values) and noncognitive constructs grounded in the theory of planned behavior (attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, intentions, and mathematics work ethic). Using SEM in Mplus with WLSMV for categorical intention indicators, the authors report that attitude determinants explain 21.1% of variance in intentions (R² = 0.211), 59.4% of variance in behavioral engagement (R² = 0.594), and 30.7% of variance in mathematics performance (R² = 0.307). The strongest structural paths are perceived behavioral control → behavioral engagement (β = 0.719) and behavioral engagement → math performance (β = 0.255), with perceived behavioral control also showing an indirect effect on performance through behavior (β = 0.184). Limitations include reliance on cross-sectional PISA data and the use of SEM rather than ML prediction; causal claims are not identified, and the study uses FIML for background missingness under MCAR assumptions.
